name: AI for Education and Learning
objectives: Given an idea you find hard, ask an AI assistant to explain it at your level with an everyday example, and say which part is still confusing, until you can explain it back in your own words
After learning an idea, ask an AI assistant for practice questions one at a time, answer them yourself and check the answers, answering before you look and checking any answer that looks wrong

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Getting a hard idea explained at your level
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask an AI assistant to explain a hard idea in a way you understand.
This lesson builds toward: Given an idea you find hard, you will ask an AI assistant to explain it at your level with an everyday example, and say which part is still confusing, until you can explain it back in your own words.
A tutor is someone who explains things one-on-one. A free AI assistant can act like a patient tutor. You can ask the same question many times, and it does not judge you.
Tell it your level: "Explain fractions like I am just starting" or "Explain it with an example about cooking." Everyday examples from your own life make ideas stick.
If it is still confusing, say what part you do not get: "I understand the first part, but not why we flip the second fraction."
Step by step:
- Name the idea you want to learn.
- Tell the AI your level and ask for an everyday example.
- Read the answer slowly.
- Say exactly which part is still confusing and ask again.
Words to know:
- Tutor: a teacher who helps one person at a time.
- Example: a real-life case that shows how an idea works.
Try it now: Pick one idea you always found hard (percentages, a grammar rule, how interest works). Ask an AI assistant to explain it at a beginner level with an example from your daily life.
You can now get a hard idea explained at your own level and ask follow-ups until it makes sense.

options: A test you take at school
check.why: A tutor helps one person learn, and an AI assistant can act like a patient one.

check.q: You get the first part of an explanation but not the second. What do you ask?
options: "I get the first part, but not why we flip the second fraction."
check.why: Saying exactly which part is confusing helps the AI explain that part.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Practicing with AI-made questions
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask an AI assistant to quiz you and check your answers.
This lesson builds toward: After learning an idea, you will ask an AI assistant for practice questions one at a time, answer them yourself and check the answers, answering before you look and checking any answer that looks wrong.
Reading is not the same as learning. You remember more when you practice: answering questions makes your brain pull the idea back out.
Ask: "Give me five practice questions about percentages, one at a time. Wait for my answer, then tell me if I am right and why."
AI can make mistakes in math and facts. If an answer looks wrong, ask it to show the steps, or check with a trusted learning site or a teacher.
Step by step:
- Ask for a small number of questions, one at a time.
- Answer each one yourself before looking anything up.
- Ask the AI to check your answer and explain.
- If its answer looks wrong, ask it to show the steps or check another source.
Words to know:
- Practice question: a question you answer to help you remember and test what you learned.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for three practice questions on the idea from Lesson 1, one at a time. Answer each one before it tells you the answer.
You can now use an AI assistant to quiz yourself and check your learning.

check.q: Why ask for practice questions one at a time?
options: The AI can only write one
You answer each one before seeing the next
check.why: One at a time lets you answer each question yourself before moving on.

check.q: The AI says 25% of 80 is 25. What do you do?
options: Ask it to show the steps or check another source
check.why: AI can make math mistakes, so you ask for the steps or check a trusted source.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Finding free learning websites
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Find a free learning website with lessons on the skill you want.
This lesson builds toward: Given a skill you want to learn, you will find a free course on a learning website or at your library, opening its first lesson.
AI is a great helper, but it is best used next to real lessons. Free learning websites give you courses in order, with videos and practice.
Khan Academy is a nonprofit with free courses in math, science, reading, economics, computing and test prep. LearnFree has free, self-paced lessons on computers, Microsoft Office, Google tools, job search, money basics, reading and math.
Your public library may also offer free classes, tutoring or online learning accounts. If you are thinking about college, ask the school's financial aid office about help paying, or look at studentaid.gov, the U.S. Department of Education's official site.
Step by step:
- Decide the skill you want to learn.
- Search for it on Khan Academy or LearnFree.
- Pick a course and look at its first lesson.
- Ask your library what free classes or tutoring it offers.
Words to know:
- Self-paced: you go at your own speed, any time of day.
- Nonprofit: an organization that works for a mission, not to make money for owners.
Official sources:
- Khan Academy: About
- LearnFree (free self-paced lessons)
- Federal Student Aid (U.S. Department of Education)
Try it now: Go to Khan Academy or LearnFree and find one course on a skill you want. Open the first lesson and write down its name.
You can now find a free learning website with a course on the skill you want.

options: Free lessons on computers, job search, money basics, reading and math
check.why: LearnFree has free, self-paced lessons on everyday skills.

check.q: You want free help learning to read better in person. Where do you ask?
check.why: Public libraries often offer free classes, tutoring or online learning accounts.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Learning that fits your life

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building a study plan that fits a busy life
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a simple two-week study plan with an AI assistant.
This lesson builds toward: Given the real time you have each week, you will create a two-week study plan with an AI assistant using one free learning site, with one small topic a day, rest days, and the plan placed where you will see it.
Many adults learn while working, raising children and caring for family. Short, steady study works better than long sessions you cannot keep up.
Ask the AI for a plan that fits your real week: "I work evenings and have 20 minutes each morning. Make a two-week plan to learn Excel basics with LearnFree. One small topic a day, with one rest day each week."
Put the plan where you will see it: on your phone calendar, on the fridge, or in a notebook. Check off each day.
Step by step:
- Choose one skill and one free learning site.
- Tell the AI how much time you have and when.
- Ask for a two-week plan with one small topic a day and rest days.
- Put it on your calendar or fridge and check off each day.
Words to know:
- Study plan: a schedule of what you will learn and when.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to make a two-week study plan for the course you found in Lesson 3, based on the real time you have each day.
You can now make a study plan that fits your real week.

check.q: Why do short, steady study sessions work for busy adults?
options: You can keep them up every day
check.why: Short sessions fit a real week, so you keep going instead of giving up.

check.q: You only have 15 minutes at lunch. What do you tell the AI when asking for a plan?
options: That you can study 3 hours a day
That you have 15 minutes at lunch each day
check.why: Telling the AI your real time lets it make a plan you can follow.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Helping a child learn without doing the work
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to help a child understand homework instead of handing them answers.
This lesson builds toward: Given a child's homework topic, you will use an AI assistant to explain the idea to you so you can teach it, without giving the child the answers, following the school's rules on AI.
AI can help you help your child, even with subjects you never learned or have forgotten. The key is to use it to explain, not to do the homework.
Schools have rules about AI. Many do not allow students to turn in work an AI wrote. Ask your child's teacher what the rules are. Also check age limits: many AI tools are only for people 13 or older, and some require a parent's permission for teens; read the tool's terms.
Good prompts for parents: "Explain how to find the area of a rectangle so I can teach my 10-year-old. Do not give the answer to this problem." Or: "Give me three easy questions to check if my child understands."
Step by step:
- Read the homework with your child.
- Ask the AI to explain the idea to you, not to solve the problem.
- Explain it to your child in your own words.
- Let your child do the work; use AI-made questions to check understanding.
- Follow the school's rules on AI use.
Words to know:
- Terms: the rules you agree to when you use an app or website, including age limits.
Try it now: Take one homework topic (or a topic from your child's grade). Ask an AI to explain it so you can teach it, without solving the problem. Write down how you would explain it in your own words.
You can now use AI to help a child learn while following school rules and keeping the work theirs.

check.q: What is the key rule for using AI with a child's homework?
options: Use it to explain, not to do the work
Let it write the whole answer
check.why: AI should help you explain the idea; your child still does the work.

check.q: Your 11-year-old wants to use an AI tool alone. What do you check first?
options: Its age limit and terms, and the school's AI rules
check.why: Many AI tools are for ages 13 and up, and schools have their own rules.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Staying on track and checking your progress
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check your own progress and adjust your plan.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of a study week, you will check your progress with a short quiz and adjust your plan, reviewing every topic you missed.
After a week, look back. Which days did you study? What can you do now that you could not do before? Small wins count.
Ask the AI to quiz you on the whole week: "I studied these five topics. Give me one question on each." The questions you miss show you what to review.
If the plan was too much, make it smaller. If it was easy, add a little. A plan that changes is still a plan.
Step by step:
- Count the days you studied.
- Ask the AI for one question on each topic you covered.
- Mark the ones you missed and review them.
- Make the plan smaller or bigger to fit your life.
Words to know:
- Progress: how far you have moved toward your goal.
- Review: going over something again to remember it better.
Try it now: Final task: make your two-week study plan with an AI assistant and one free learning site, then ask for five practice questions on the first topic, answer them yourself, and check your answers.
You can now learn a new skill with a study plan, free lessons and AI practice, and adjust as you go.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Free learning site No learning site, or a paid one. Names one free learning site and the course or lessons used. Also names a free class or tutoring option at the library. Two-week plan No plan, or a plan that does not fit the learner's real time. Two weeks, about 20 minutes a day, one small topic a day, with rest days. Placed on a calendar or the fridge with days checked off. Practice questions Looked at the answers first, or did not answer the questions. Five questions answered before checking, and each one checked. Asked the AI to show steps on any answer that looked wrong. Progress check No look back at what was missed. Lists the questions missed and what to review. Says how the plan will change based on the results. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What do the questions you miss on a weekly quiz show you?
check.why: Missed questions point to the topics to review.

check.q: Your plan felt too easy this week. What do you do?
options: Add a little more to the plan
check.why: A plan should change to fit you; if it is easy, add a little.
